title: A Chef's Meditation on Feeding Strangers Well
script: Narrator: [warmly] Twenty years behind a stove taught me that hospitality collapses the instant it starts calculating who deserves the good cuts of meat.
Narrator: [reflective] I've fed critics who reviewed me harshly and fed strangers who wandered in penniless, and I've tried, imperfectly, to plate both meals with identical attention.
Narrator: [honest] Tried, I say, because the temptation to punish a bad review with a mediocre second dish is considerably stronger than any cookbook ever admits openly.
Narrator: [wry] I've indulged that temptation exactly once, early in my career, and the resulting dish tasted precisely as resentful as I felt while plating it.
Narrator: [thoughtful] Adab in a kitchen, I've come to think, isn't primarily about technique, however much technique dominates the actual training we receive.
Narrator: [reflective] It's about extending the same unhurried attention to the guest who can't afford dessert as to the one settling a considerable bill without glancing at it twice.
Narrator: [honest] My grandmother, who ran a considerably humbler kitchen than mine, used to say a guest's hunger doesn't announce itself according to their income.
Narrator: [warmly] I didn't understand that as instruction until years into my own career, plating food for people whose worth I'd begun, quietly, ranking by their tips alone.
Narrator: [reflective] Ranking guests, I eventually noticed, is a peculiar kind of theft, taking something that was never mine to withhold selectively in the first place.
Narrator: [thoughtful] The example set toward guests in our tradition was never calibrated to their status, and I've spent considerable effort since trying, imperfectly, to plate accordingly.
Narrator: [gently] Some nights the kitchen is chaos, tickets stacking faster than we can manage, and generosity becomes the first casualty of that particular chaos.
Narrator: [determined] On those nights I try hardest, not because generosity comes easily under pressure, but precisely because it doesn't, and that's rather when it counts most.
Narrator: [peacefully] Every plate that leaves my kitchen, I hope, carries less of my judgment about who deserves it and more of whatever hospitality actually requires of me.

quiz.question: What did twenty years behind a stove teach the narrator about hospitality?
options: That hospitality should focus on wealthy guests only
That hospitality collapses the instant it starts calculating who deserves the good cuts of meat
That hospitality is unrelated to how food is served
That hospitality only matters for critics
quiz.explanation: He learned hospitality collapses the moment it starts calculating who deserves the good cuts of meat.

quiz.question: What happened the one time the narrator gave in to the temptation to punish a bad reviewer?
options: The dish turned out perfectly regardless
The resulting dish tasted precisely as resentful as he felt while plating it
He was praised for his honesty
Nothing different happened at all
quiz.explanation: He indulged the temptation once and the dish tasted precisely as resentful as he felt while making it.

quiz.question: What did the narrator's grandmother used to say about a guest's hunger?
options: That it only matters for paying customers
That a guest's hunger doesn't announce itself according to their income
That hunger should be ignored during busy nights
That only regular customers deserve full attention
quiz.explanation: His grandmother said a guest's hunger doesn't announce itself according to their income.

quiz.question: What does the narrator call the practice of ranking guests by their tips?
options: A necessary business practice
A peculiar kind of theft, taking something that was never his to withhold selectively
An acceptable part of running a restaurant
Something his grandmother taught him to do
quiz.explanation: He calls ranking guests a peculiar kind of theft, taking something never his to withhold selectively.

quiz.question: When does the narrator say he tries hardest to be generous?
options: Only on slow, calm nights
On chaotic nights, precisely because generosity doesn't come easily under pressure
Only when critics are present
He says generosity never varies by circumstance
quiz.explanation: He tries hardest on chaotic nights, because generosity doesn't come easily under pressure, which is when it counts most.
